docs.title: GLUE Connector Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome! This is the documentation of the Github project GLUE Connector.

GLUE stands for General and Lightweight Usage Enforcement. Our connector can enforce secure usage control for data pipelines executed on a remote cloud system. The following sections provide insights and different entry points to our documentation.

Introduction provides an overview and the motivation of the GLUE project.

Getting Started details the first steps to get the system running quickly.

Concept Overview illustrates the technical components which make up the architecture.

Concept Deed-Dive further explains the technical architecture with additional information.

Use Cases summarizes different use-cases which all require usage control and can be realized with the GLUE connector.

Containers and their Functions lists the available standard containers which work out-of-the-box.

Network Exposure explains how the connector and its pipelines are reached by other connectors.

docs.title: Connector Architecture
docs.text:
| Connector deployment with supporting services. Insecure deployments do not include components in grey. |

The figure above shows the services involved in each connector deployment as well as their interactions with each other as well as with the external service containers. Alongside the GLUE Connector itself, we deploy a separate docker daemon for each connector. The GLUE Connector uses this docker daemon to manage individual pipeline containers.

The Container Measurement Component (CMC) provides cross-platform attestation capabilities via its API, which we use to attest the connectors. Trust anchor is either the Trusted Execution Environment's hardware used for measuring the software stack or a Trusted Platform Module (TPM). In our examples we use a software TPM to serve as the attestation backend for the CMC. The CMC also manages the TLS certificate we use in the connector. It fetches these certificates via Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) from the EST server.

docs.title: Transitive Usage Control
docs.text:
The core idea behind GLUE is to enforce usage control rules by restricting access to protected data to processors specified in a policy. The data owner is able to trust that the terms of the policy are followed through attestation before providing any data, even if more than one party is involved. The figure above shows an exemplary data processing scenario in the GLUE system.

At each operator, the received data enters a local pipeline, which must conform to the restrictions defined in the instantiated policy. When the derived data is going to be forwarded to connected operators, the GLUE usage control engine instantiates a Policy Template by replacing the placeholders with the parameters provided by the current pipeline containers. Thereby, GLUE establishes a new usage control policy that governs the processing steps at the subsequent operator's organization. Only the data that the sub-policy designates as permitted output is released from GLUE control to the end consumers, while any remaining protected data remains under usage control enforcement. By nesting this approach, GLUE enforces usage control rules across an arbitrary number of processing steps.

docs.title: Connection Sequence
docs.text:
The sequence of steps necessary to setup a GLUE pipeline are denoted in the figure above. The steps include: 1. Remote attestation of the software stack which carries the GLUE connector and all involved parts. 2. The contract for data processing is negotiated. 3. The GLUE connector initializes the specified container pipeline. 4. The data source now sends data to the GLUE connector.

The transitve pipeline is started by one GLUE connector establishing an additional transitive pipeline to another GLUE connector.

  1. Remote attestation is performed again as in step 1.
  2. A sub-contract is negotiated according to the rules specified in the primary policy.
  3. The second GLUE connector initialises the appropriate second data processing pipeline.
  4. The derived result data from the first pipeline is sent to the 2nd GLUE connector.

In the end, the data must be released to a data receiver.

  1. The data sink is attested in order to guarantee a secure release environment.
  2. Currently, one pipeline can only pass data into another pipeline. Therefore, the data sink acts as another pipeline with release logic for the data output, which may be triggered using a pull reqest.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: A transitive GLUE pipeline can typically be deployed among different Trusted Execution Environments as depicted in the figure above. Not all GLUE connector have to be on the same system. Each endpoint and starting points need to remotely attest each other to enable a fully trusted, usage controlled combination of data processing pipelines.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text: The GLUE connector uses the widely used, standardized ODRL format. While ODRL provides a comprehensive model for expressing usage rights through rules, constraints, and obligations, it lacks concepts for GLUE’s data processing pipelines and transitively negotiated contracts. Therefore, the standard format is extended with additional dedicated attributes and concepts specifically designed for the GLUE connector as shown in the figures below. For instance, Data Processing Pipelines were added for representing data processing workflows in usage control policies. The figure above shows the simplified overview. The figure below shows the "ODRL Core Profile Information Model" extended with classes from the GLUE custom profile, which is a detailed complete overview of the extension.

docs.title: Pipeline Layout
docs.text:
As shown above, a GLUE data pipeline consists of three elements:

  • a defined data input port (DIP),
  • one or more data processing steps (DPS), and
  • a defined data output port (DOP).

Input and output ports specify permitted port mappings and protocols for data transfer and result retrieval. Each processing step is uniquely identified by a cryptographic hash covering its software artifact, including binaries, configuration, and initial data.

Unlike approaches that model only abstract algorithms, GLUE represents concrete processing steps as software artifacts. Multiple steps can be chained to compose complex pipelines combining processing operations and protocol adapters.

Data processing pipelines are modeled as a subtype of the ODRL RightOperand class, allowing them to be used in ODRL constraints and action refinements. Constraints can restrict which pipelines may process an asset, while action refinements can require a specific pipeline to be executed. For this purpose, the GLUE profile introduces the deployPipeline action, which the framework executes on behalf of the data owner.

docs.title: Full Component Overview
docs.text:
The figure above shows a detailed architecture overview of a two-level transitive data processing pipeline. The data flow originates at the Provider VM on the left, passas through the Intermediary VM, and ultimately ends in the Consumer VM on the right hand side. Each of the VMs makes use of confidential computing, as they all need to be executed inside a trusted execution environment, here denoted in green. The software artifacts, which are necessary for managing the pipeline and contract negotiation are marked in white boxes with a black border. Dynamically spawned containers, each depending on the given policy, are shown in blue boxes.

For a simplified view the components for remote attestation are neglected, however, during connection setup each VM has to attest the next peer before a data transmission can begin, as denoted using arrows at the top. The contract negotiation component has to be available in each GLUE connector and addresses the negotiation from one peer to the next. The UC/Pipeline manager issues policies and controls the container deployment manager. The container deployment manager deploys and configures the containers of each pipeline. The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) has to be available within each container, however, in GLUE the PEP is indirectly implemented by the available logic of containers and enforced by feature availablity.

docs.title: General Concept Overview
docs.text: This section provides an abstract overview of the involved parties and the main architecture of the GLUE framework.

docs.title: Concept Overview
docs.text: GLUE makes use of a Confidential VM (CVM), which is a TEE-protected VM. The CVM contains a Docker engine inside. The GLUE connector orchestrates the instantiation of a data processing pipeline consisting of chained docker containers with highly restricted permissions in a processing chain. Data may only enter into the first container, here C1, and may only leave the usage controlled environment at the last container, here C4. Either C4 implements a data output as reply to a previous user request or the data is forwarded into another pipeline. The usage controlled area is denoted in green and under full control of the parties which agreed upon the corresponding data processing policy.

docs.title: Layered Overview
docs.text:
This section details an overview separated into control and data plane as shown in the following figure.

First, two connectors negotiate a policy on the control plane. The policy defines permitted containers and data flows that must be adhered to during the data process. Then the connector spawns a local pipeline which implements the exact data flow from the policy. The respective Docker engine must use hash measurements to prove that the correct containers are running unchanged. The respective configurations of the containers is also generated from parameters in the policy. The whitelisting of docker containers and their data processing order narrows down the acceptable data flow and is enforced by the framework.

The control plane deals with the negotiation of accepted policies. The format applied is ODRL, more information about the topic can be found in Concept Deep-Dive. The data plane focusses only on the transmission of datasets. This is the plane, where the GLUE connector launches, attests and enforces the previously agreed upon data processing pipelines. The data flow must be implemented directly in the form of a chain (or a directed graph which is currently future work) from one container to the next.

docs.title: List of Containers for Container-based and pipelined Usage-Control (CoPi-UC)
docs.text: The GLUE Connector provides numerous precompiled instances of example containers to be used inside processing chains. We currently host our example containers on Docker Hub.

docs.title: Available Containers
docs.text: This section details containers which are already available of usage in a pipeline processing network.

docs.title: Data-Retrieval-Container (Start-Container)
docs.text: Start container that handles the reception of data and also provides buffer options for larger amounts of data. - Serves as only accepted input to a processing network.

docs.title: Data-Release-Container (End-Container)
docs.text: End container that enables the final output of the data to clearly predefined interfaces. - Visualization output - Data output - Binary output

docs.title: Filter-Container
docs.text: The container is configured via a configurable regular expression to dynamically delete special records. Example: records for a specific group must be removed.

docs.title: Anonymizer-Container
docs.text: The container deletes personal data. Example: reliable deletion of first name or last name fields.

docs.title: Attribute-Reference-Protection-Container
docs.text:
If certain data records are personally identifiable, they must be deleted or the property must be removed. Example: a single female entry is the only one in the data set.

Typical technics for protection against attribute inference make use of: - K-Anonimity - L-Diversity - T-Closeness - and more privacy configuration factors

docs.title: Future Containers
docs.text: This section details containers which are planned for usage in a pipeline processing network and will be implemented soon.

docs.title: Loop-Container
docs.text: Repeats processes in a flow of programs until a certain condition is met on the data sets.

docs.title: Jump-Container
docs.text: Executes program jumps to configurable positions in a container chain.

docs.title: Label-Container
docs.text: A container that can provide datasets with an additional label as meta information.

docs.title: JSON-Modification-Container
docs.text: A container that can change the format of the data in a configurable manner.

docs.title: Database-Container / a.k.a. Aggregation-Container
docs.text: Extraction tester: e.g. At least 10 data sets (protection against extraction) Selectable mass operation on fields (e.g. average, sum, variance)

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The project documentation you are currently reading is part of the GLUE Connector repository on GitHub. Its source code resiedes in the docs/ directory. When documentation changes are merged into main, the documentation page is updated automatically by GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Compilation of Project Documentation
docs.text:
As with any code contributions, changes to the documentation must be built and tested before contributing. The following command may be used to compile the documentation and place the rendered outputs under site/

docker compose -f docker-compose.docs.yml run --rm mkdocs build -f .github/mkdocs.yml

The following Compose file must be present at the repository root as docker-compose.docs.yml.

name: glue-documentation

services:
  mkdocs:
    image: squidfunk/mkdocs-material:9
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - ./:/docs
    command: serve -f .github/mkdocs.yml --dev-addr=0.0.0.0:8000

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
The GLUE repository contains a simple examples for demonstration. The corresponding code can be seen here: GLUE Examples.

This directory contains examples for the deployment of the GLUE Connector. The examples use docker compose to orchestrate the required components as containers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Running the example requires docker compose, openssl, yq, jo, envsubst, curl, and skopeo. We assume that a docker daemon is already available and that you have access to it. Podman may also work, but we do not officially support it. In addition to the dependencies, the examples require that port 5000 is available on the host machine.

docs.title: Debian-based systems
docs.text:
The installation command assumes that the official docker repository is configured.

apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin openssl yq jo gettext-base curl skopeo

docs.title: Arch Linux
docs.text: pacman -S docker docker-buildx docker-compose openssl yq jo gettext curl skopeo

docs.title: Nix Shell
docs.text: nix-shell -p docker-client docker-buildx docker-compose openssl yq jo gettext curl skopeo

docs.title: Running Examples
docs.text:
To demonstrate the different capabilities of the GLUE Connector, we provide a set of examples. Each example defines its own actors and policy that may deploy different pipeline configurations. To start an example, run ./example.sh <example> or run ./example.sh --help for more information on its complete functionality. Possible options for <example> can be seen in the example folder. As chosen example multi-stage is used in the next explanation.

Basic Multi-Stage Example: The multi-stage example showcases a data processing chain consisting of three connectors each running a separate processing pipeline. The first connector (initiator) negotiates a contract with the second connector (intermediary), which then performs a follow-up negotiation with the final connector (destination). The follow-up policy is defined statically in the initial policy without dynamic parameters. Run this example with ./example.sh multi-stage.

docs.title: Example Internals
docs.text: This section provides a short overview of the example infrastructure's internal workings. It details how each connector is represented within the docker compose environment, what parts are included as infrastructure components and how the attestation is performed in the example.

docs.title: Connector Deployment
docs.text:
All examples consist of one or more connector deployments and a set of supporting infrastructure. We deploy each service in a separate docker container and link them together where necessary. In a production deployment, each connector would consist of a single confidential VM with the required services running directly on the system. We use the docker compose depends_on and healthcheck features to make sure that services start in the correct order. Related services communicate via a linked network namespace as well as a dedicated shared volume where we place shared sockets and files.

Figure 1: Connector deployment with supporting services. Insecure deployments do not include components in grey.

Figure 1 shows the services involved in each connector deployment as well as their interactions with each other as well as with the external service containers. Alongside the GLUE Connector itself, we deploy a separate docker daemon for each connector. The GLUE Connector uses this docker daemon to manage individual pipeline containers. To ensure that the examples work in any environment, we bundle all container images and load them into a local container registry on startup.

The Container Measurement Component (CMC) provides cross-platform attestation capabilities via its API, which we use to attest the connectors. We use a software TPM to serve as the attestation backend for the CMC. The CMC also manages the TLS certificate we use in the connector. It fetches these certificates via Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) from the EST server. When using the --insecure flag, these containers are not used or created.

docs.title: What just happened?
docs.text: The docker compose script above starts a sample container setup which allows the enforcement of usage control. The same data processing network can be launched on a remote system.

docs.title: More Information
docs.text:
More information about the provided examples, how they can be modified and further details of the configurable parameters can be found in the GLUE Examples.

See the Concept Overview for more information on the concepts and design decisions underlying the GLUE Connector.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The GLUE connector was built for usage control of container pipelines. The following sections provide insights about the motivation, the concepts used, and a simplified explanation of our approach. More technical details are explained in the following sections Concept Overview and Concept Deed-Dive.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Nowadays, more and more workloads are moved to remote cloud systems for several reasons including lower cost, dynamic load balancing capabilities, managed administration, or for financial benefits, as no self-hosted hardware is needed. However, using a remote system for data processing requires trusting the cloud provider. To enable trust our system makes use of two security paradigms which are Confidential Computing and Usage Control.

Confidential Computing is a term which states that an execution remains private and protected and only visible to a remote peer controlling the process. It typically makes use of Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to execute code in a protected realm on a remote computer while still making it impossible for even root-level administrators to interfere with the sandboxed execution.

Usage control can control the flow of data beyond traditional access control. Access control determines who is allowed to access data, but once access is granted, it typically does not control what the recipient can do with it. Usage control is therefore needed to enforce ongoing constraints on how data may be processed, transformed, forwarded, or shared after access has been granted. Constraints for data processing are kept not just during the moment of transmission, but even after the sets of data have left the data provider. The most typical constraints include: - Time frames: allowing the usage of data during a certain period - Purposes: allowing only a pre-defined set of actions, which the data may be used for after its transmission. - Geolocation: restricting the processing of data for certain countries or areas

Using these paradigm numerous new use cases can be realized, which are detailed in our section about Use Cases. The ultimate aim is to enable the processing of data on a remote cloud system according to accepted policies among multiple peers without having security drawbacks, such as data leaks, while still profiting from cloud benefits. We address this scenario using our GLUE connector which is capable to control and enforce usage control policies.

docs.title: Our Approach
docs.text:
In our design we provide a usage control framework for enforcing a policy-bound pipeline of containers for data processing. On the one hand, we gain dynamic usage control, since we can plug together any container as desired. On the other hand we remain in full control of the enforcement of the usage control due to the precisely defined acceptable data flows within the container network, which are bound in a corresponding policy.

For a practical guide to set up the GLUE Connector, see the Getting Started Guide. To gain a deeper insight into the underlying concepts and design decisions, see Concept Overview Section.

docs.title: Network Exposure
docs.text: This page describes which ports a GLUE connector opens and how other connectors reach the pipelines it runs. It also lists the options that set the public addresses of both.

docs.title: Connector Ports
docs.text:
Port Purpose 8080 User-facing API for starting negotiations and managing pipelines. Do not expose it publicly. 8444 Inter-connector (DSP) API for negotiations between connectors, secured with (attested) TLS.

Other connectors only need to reach port 8444, at the address set in connector.publicUrl.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Option Environment variable Default Description connector.publicUrl PUBLIC_URL local IP address Public URL of the inter-connector API. connector.pipelineHost PIPELINE_HOST host of publicUrl Host under which other connectors reach this connector's pipelines. sniProxy.enabled SNI_PROXY_ENABLED false Expose pipelines through an SNI proxy instead of publishing their ports. sniProxy.port SNI_PROXY_PORT port of publicUrl Public port of the SNI proxy that is announced to other connectors. docker.sniProxyNetwork SNI_PROXY_NETWORK sni-proxy Docker network shared by the SNI proxy and the pipeline entry containers.

docs.title: Pipeline Exposure
docs.text: Every pipeline has an entry container that listens on port 8080 inside the container. This port is exposed in one of two ways.

docs.title: Port Publishing (default)
docs.text: Docker publishes the entry port on a free host port from the kernel's ephemeral port range (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, usually 32768-60999). Other connectors reach the pipeline at <pipelineHost>:<port>, so the whole ephemeral range must be reachable.

docs.title: SNI Proxy
docs.text: With sniProxy.enabled, a TLS passthrough proxy that routes by SNI, such as Envoy, HAProxy or Traefik, fronts all pipelines on a single port. Every pipeline gets the hostname <pipelineId>.<pipelineHost>. Other connectors connect to <pipelineId>.<pipelineHost>:<sniProxy.port>, which requires a wildcard DNS record for *.<pipelineHost>. The proxy resolves the same hostname on the network docker.sniProxyNetwork and forwards the connection to the entry container's port 8080. sniProxy.port is only the port announced to other connectors. It does not have to match the port the proxy itself listens on, for example when the proxy is behind a port forwarding.

docs.title: Appendix: Minimal Envoy Configuration
docs.text:
This configuration assumes connector.publicUrl=https://glue.example.org:8444 (and therefore the default connector.pipelineHost=glue.example.org) and an Envoy container attached to docker.sniProxyNetwork. The Envoy container must also be able to reach the connector under the name connector.

static_resources:
  listeners:
    - name: tls
      address:
        socket_address: { address: 0.0.0.0, port_value: 8444 }
      listener_filters:
        - name: envoy.filters.listener.tls_inspector
          typed_config:
            "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.listener.tls_inspector.v3.TlsInspector
      filter_chains:
        - filter_chain_match:
            server_names: ["glue.example.org"]
          filters:
            - name: envoy.filters.network.tcp_proxy
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.tcp_proxy.v3.TcpProxy
                stat_prefix: connector
                cluster: connector
        - filter_chain_match:
            server_names: ["*.glue.example.org"]
          filters:
            - name: envoy.filters.network.sni_dynamic_forward_proxy
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.sni_dynamic_forward_proxy.v3.FilterConfig
                port_value: 8080
                dns_cache_config: { name: pipelines }
            - name: envoy.filters.network.tcp_proxy
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.tcp_proxy.v3.TcpProxy
                stat_prefix: pipelines
                cluster: pipelines
  clusters:
    - name: connector
      type: STRICT_DNS
      load_assignment:
        cluster_name: connector
        endpoints:
          - lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address: { address: connector, port_value: 8444 }
    - name: pipelines
      lb_policy: CLUSTER_PROVIDED
      cluster_type:
        name: envoy.clusters.dynamic_forward_proxy
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.clusters.dynamic_forward_proxy.v3.ClusterConfig
          dns_cache_config: { name: pipelines }

docs.title: 3. Transfer of Data

If we transfer personal data collected through websites to processors, we will notify you in this data protection information regarding the respective data processing operation, citing the specific recipient.

Aside from that, we will transfer your personal data only if

  • you have given explicit consent pursuant to Art. 6 (1) lit. a GDPR;
  • this is necessary pursuant to Article 6 (1) lit. b GDPR for the performance of a contract with you (for example, transfer to shipping companies for the purpose of delivering goods ordered by you, or transmitting payment information to payment service providers or credit institutions in order to process a payment transaction);
  • there is a legal obligation for transfer pursuant to Art. 6 (1) lit. c GDPR.

The recipients must not use the transferred data for any purposes other than the above-mentioned ones.

docs.title: 4. Rights of the Data Subject
docs.text:
You have the right:

  • pursuant to Art. 7(3) GDPR, to withdraw your consent at any time. This means that we may not continue the data processing based on this consent in the future;
  • pursuant to Art. 15 GDPR, to obtain access to your personal data processed by us. In particular, you may request information about the purposes of the processing, the categories of personal data concerned, the categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed, and the envisaged period for which the data will be stored. Moreover, you have the right to request rectification, erasure, or restriction of processing, to object to processing, the right to lodge a complaint, and to obtain information about the source of your data if they were not collected by us as well as about the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, and, if applicable, meaningful information about the details involved;
  • pursuant to Art. 16 GDPR, to obtain without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate data or the completion of your personal data stored by us;
  • pursuant to Art. 17 GDPR, to obtain the erasure of personal data stored by us unless processing is necessary to exercise the right of freedom of expression and information, to comply with a legal obligation, for reasons of public interest, or to establish, exercise or defend legal claims;
  • pursuant to Art. 18 GDPR, to obtain restriction of processing of your personal data if you contest the accuracy of the data, the processing is unlawful but you oppose the erasure of the personal data, or if we no longer need the personal data while you still require it for establishing, exercising or defending legal claims, or if you have filed an objection to the processing pursuant to Art. 21 GDPR;
  • pursuant to Art. 20 GDPR, to receive your personal data that you have provided to us, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format or to demand the transfer of those data to another controller and
  • pursuant to Art. 77 GDPR, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. Generally, you may contact the supervisory authority of your usual residence, place of work or the registered offices of our organization.

docs.title: 5. Information on your right to object pursuant to Art. 21 GDPR
docs.text:
You have the right to object, on grounds relating to your particular situation, at any time to processing of your personal data pursuant to Art. 6 (1) lit. e GDPR (data processing carried out in the public interest) and Art. 6 (1) lit. f GDPR (data processing for purposes of legitimate interests). This also applies to any profiling as defined in Art. 4 (4) GDPR that is based on said provision in Art. 6.

If you file an objection, we will no longer process your personal data unless we can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds for processing that override your interests, rights and freedoms, or unless the processing serves the establishment, exercise or defense of legal claims.

If your objection is directed against the processing of data for the purpose of direct advertising, we will stop the processing immediately. In this case, citing a special situation is not necessary. This includes profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct advertising.

If you would like to assert your right to object, simply send an email to datenschutzkoordination(at)zv.fraunhofer.de.

docs.title: 6. Data Security
docs.text:
All your personal data are transmitted in encrypted format, using the widely used and secure TLS (Transport Layer Security) standard. TLS is a secure and proven standard that is also used, for instance, in online banking. You will recognize a secure TLS connection by the additional s after http (i.e., https://...) in the address bar of your browser or by the lock icon in the bottom part of your browser window.

In all other regards, we use suitable technical and organizational security measures to protect your data against accidental or intentional manipulations, partial or complete loss, destruction, or the unauthorized access of third parties. We continuously improve our security measures in accordance with the state of the art.

docs.title: 7. Timeliness and Amendments to this Data Protection Information
docs.text: The further development of our website and the products and services offered or changed due to statutory or regulatory requirements, respectively, may make it necessary to amend this data protection information. You may access and print out the latest data protection information at any time from our website.

docs.title: List of Use Cases für Usage Control
docs.text: The following are examples of Usage Control that can be realized using our GLUE Connector.

docs.title: Usase Control for Generation of Cyber-Threat-Intelligence (CTI)
docs.text:
Scenario: Multiple Security Operation Centers (SOCs) all collect data individually in their domain.

Problem: Analyzing alert data is required to generate advanced Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) for more parties or even the public domain. However, alert data is extremely sensitive as it may harm the organization which is put under surveillance, if the data is leaked. Also, due to legal restrictions, SOCs typically are not allowed to share any alert data.

Solution: A usage controlled CTI process which may collect data from multiple SOCs with predifined processing procedures can enable collaborative CTI. The predefined processing procedures include functional checks, the processing of the data, inference protection, and the regulated release of output results according a procedure which all participants have previously agreed upon via policy agreement.

docs.title: Usage Control for Medical Data
docs.text:
Scenario: Patients share their data with government agencies or hospitals to receive analytical services. Government agencies or medical organizations store this sensitive data in the cloud and are only allowed to pass it on under very strict conditions.

Problem: Medical data is often extremely sensitive data. Access to this data is often only possible under very strict regulations and passing it on is usually completely prohibited. Nevertheless, there is often a need to combine datasets of patients from different disease measurements from different hospitals, organizations or companies in order to gain special insights from the data.

Solution: With confidential computing coupled with usage control enforcement, an architecture can be designed in which everyone involved can trust that access to the data is regulated according to imposed restrictions. On the one hand, the data providers can be sure that the raw data cannot be extracted. On the other hand, studies, aggregations, or combinations of data can be compiled from multiple sources that would otherwise not be legally or technically feasible. The main condition is that the results of the operations or analyzes do not provide any indications of the raw data and are filtered accordingly.

docs.title: Usage Control for Governmental Data
docs.text:
[!NOTE] Wahrscheinlich hauptsächlich meine persönliche Meinung, aber mit Wahlen als Anwendungsfall macht man schon ein Fass auf. Es darf nirgendwo stehen, wer was gewählt hat, was man aber für Analysen braucht.

Rep: Naja gerade das zu lösen ist ja gerade unten beschrieben.

Scenario: Citizens pass on their election data, i.e. votes, to government ballot boxes. The government must archive all election records and ensure that this sensitive data is only permitted for certain analyses.

Problem: Analyses that draw conclusions about voter behavior, such as changing votes or demographic and regional analyses, require insight into the raw data. However, this is typically not allowed or desired by the governmental agency which must protect the privacy of the voters.

Solution: With confidential computing, coupled with usage control enforcement, an architecture can be designed in which everyone involved can trust that access to the data is only permitted in ways that ensure anonymity of voters and their privacy. Sensitive election data can be collected and combined from different government agencies and different states without having to reveal the raw data. More complex algorithms for a more comprehensive and precise analysis of voter behavior can be secured using usage control than would be the case with conventional projections.

docs.title: Usage Control in Industrial Manufacturing
docs.text:
Scenario:

Companies with blueprints for manufacturing and production factories belong to different parties. Either the companies want to perform contract manufacturing, where the factory is owned by a third party, or the third party needs components for their machines and equipment, but on-site production is faster than delayed delivery. In any case, product owners of these products do not want to give up their intellectual property, i.e. the blueprints for manufacturing them.

Problem: Sharing the blueprint would effectively nullify competitive advantages gained through their development. Nevertheless, the components should be able to be manufactured on site.

Solution: An architecture incorporating usage control and remote attestation of production machines' firmware enables blueprints to be sent safely and securely to an on-site confidential VM and stored there in RAM inaccessible to the outside world. Only the remotely attested machine is able to receive instructions for production from this VM, which is also remotely attested and secured by the data provider. A reconstruction of the previously sent blueprint can only be done using lower quality methods, such as 3D scanning of the finished printed object with smoothing calculations and rounding errors. In this way, a company would be able to produce products on site and rent the blueprints in a technically secure manner for a predetermined number of printing processes.
